text: I looked at every painting in the room.
The light comes from the left, and everything depends on it.
Your draft is 812 words. The limit is 650. How do you feel about losing 162 of them?
Honestly? Like someone is asking me to choose which fingers to keep.
Then let us not start with fingers. Let us start with fingernails. Look at your second paragraph.
It says, it is important to note that at that particular moment in time I made the decision to step back.
How would you say that out loud to a friend?
At that moment, I stepped back. Oh. That is twenty words gone and nothing lost.
Exactly. Do that to every paragraph before you touch a single idea. Now, the sentence about the guard warning you four times stays.
Even if it is a bit long?
It is the only sentence in the essay that nobody else could have written. When I edit, that is the sentence I protect.
So I cut the padding around my voice, not my voice.
Cut words before sentences, and sentences before ideas.
Concision is not brevity; it is the absence of waste.
Cut the padding around your voice, not your voice.
Every word you keep has to earn its place.

Thank you for having me at the festival. I have edited magazine pieces for almost twenty years, and I want to tell you a secret about every writer I have ever worked with, including the famous ones. Every one of them believes that every word in their first draft is necessary. And every one of them is wrong, usually by about ten percent. So here is the exercise I give young writers, and I would love you to try it this week. Before you send anything to anyone, a school essay, an application, an email to a teacher, cut ten percent of it. But here is the rule. You are not allowed to remove a single idea. Only words. You will be amazed at how often you can do it. And one more thing, because people confuse these two ideas constantly. A short piece is not the same as a concise piece. A short piece simply has few words. A concise piece has no wasted ones. That means a long essay can be perfectly concise, and a short one can be full of padding.

Okay, let's talk about word limits, because I know exactly how most of you feel about them. You see a limit of six hundred and fifty words as a punishment, or at least as an obstacle standing between you and everything you want to say. I would like to persuade you that it is closer to a gift. A word limit forces you to do the hardest and most important part of writing, which is deciding what actually matters. Without a limit, you can put everything in and let the reader sort it out. With one, you have to sort it out yourself. So when your draft is too long, and it will be, cut in this order. Words first: the redundant phrases, the empty openings, the weak verbs. Then sentences. And whole ideas only at the very end, when there is truly nothing else left to remove. Most of the time, you will reach the limit before you ever get to that last step, and you will not have lost anything you care about.
Because I was standing too close, the guard warned me.
The first draft was verbose, not wrong.
The paragraph about the bus ride is extraneous.
Remove the padding before you remove the ideas.
Cut words before sentences, and sentences before ideas.
Concision is not brevity; it is the absence of waste.
The sentence is grammatically correct but cumbersome.
Excise the sentence that explains what the scene already shows.
Every word you keep has to earn its place.
Cut the padding around your voice, not your voice.
